content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered lawn mower with a robotic mower controlled by an iPhone. You need to manually drive the machine around the perimeter of the yard, and it will create a virtual map. Once setup is complete, it automatically handles the mowing according to a set schedule.

Recently, I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation approach, and after several weeks of testing, I feel it may be a more convenient and user-friendly option for many people.

Camera-based automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. The setup process required me to manually drive the mower around the perimeter with my phone in order to create an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses what the manufacturer calls the TerraVision 2.0 system. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map out the lawn, without the need to lay underground boundary wires or install a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method takes noticeably longer to create the initial map. But I feel it may be simpler for people who aren't particularly tech-savvy.

To test this theory, I had my mom, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She replied that everything worked fine. I was more skeptical about whether she would have the patience to manually drive the robot around the perimeter and manually mark off areas to avoid.

Automatic mapping did introduce one small quirk in my front yard. Because there's no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbor's, the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbor's grass in my map.

I resolved this by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there are no clear visual boundaries between lawns, you need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping.

Seeing the world through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favorite features. The iPhone app can display a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to open this feed in a large window. I could work indoors while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the backyard.

This feature isn't necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting and can occasionally help explain why it slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps share a lot of similarities in other respects. Both can schedule jobs, adjust mowing modes, set up zones, mark no-go areas, and remotely control the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly well-designed feature for that last function. In addition to traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a one-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the primary use of either system. Ideally, the robot should follow the schedule and not require any manual operation. However, TerraMow's joystick is very handy for cleaning up areas that were missed.

Sometimes, it feels almost like I'm controlling the robot with my mind (in a pleasant way). I can hold the iPhone down at my side, make slight movements with my thumb, and the machine follows my direction.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control method.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and generated more noise while operating.

I wouldn't describe the TerraMow as loud. It's just that the difference between the two is noticeable. The Anthbot can operate so quietly that it's easy to forget it's running, even when it continues mowing after sunset using its headlight.

Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. This makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy. It's also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for several consecutive weeks without needing to do the typical mowing work myself.

When smart mapping gets too smart

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up occasionally works against it.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each session takes some time, during which you can't do anything else in the app.

After several consecutive days of rain, I encountered an interesting edge case. Water pooled in part of the yard, and the TerraMow sensibly avoided that area during its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular area grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret this growth as something to continue avoiding, and even after the ground had dried, that patch of grass was never touched again.

I used the remote control feature in the app to manually drive over the taller grass and resolved the issue. Once that patch resumed looking like a normal lawn, automatic mowing resumed there as usual.

Regular edge trimming also helps the TerraMow confidently reach boundary areas. Tall grass growing along unclear boundaries may otherwise be mistaken as obstacles and excluded from the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids situations where the map changes its mind about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac Opinion

After using both systems, I lean toward TerraMow's camera approach for most people.

Underground boundary wires are completely unworkable for me, and installing an RTK base station means one more piece of hardware to position, power, and maintain. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't perfect. The initial mapping takes longer, invisible boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behavior once mistook overgrown grass as a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In exchange, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, a captivating real-time camera view, and the best manual controls I've seen in any robotic mower app.

I actually enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. After handing off this task to a robot, I have more time for landscaping, edging, and detailed trimming while still keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does this well enough that I can recommend it, especially for anyone who wants to use a robotic mower but doesn't want to dig trenches and bury wires, install an RTK antenna, or manually walk the entire perimeter of the yard with their phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon for US$999 after applying a US$200 coupon on the website. You can also purchase it from TerraMow's official website.
